config.title: Test Error Boundary

intro.title: Test Error Boundary
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React application that intentionally triggers an error to test an Error Boundary component. You will learn how Error Boundaries catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree, log those errors, and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app. The main technologies involved are React's class components (for the Error Boundary) and TypeScript for type safety. By the end, you'll understand how to create and use an Error Boundary to make your React apps more resilient.
intro.usecase: Error boundaries are essential in production React applications to prevent entire dashboards or interfaces from crashing when a single component fails. For example, in a financial dashboard displaying multiple data visualizations, an error in one chart component shouldn't bring down the entire dashboard—the error boundary would catch it and show a fallback UI while other charts remain functional. Similarly, in e-commerce product pages with multiple interactive sections (reviews, recommendations, specifications), error boundaries isolate failures to specific sections, maintaining overall page usability. This pattern is crucial for maintaining user trust and application stability when unexpected errors occur in complex, component-rich interfaces.

objectives: Apply TypeScript interfaces to define the expected props structure for an Error Boundary component.
Implement class component syntax with React.Component to create an Error Boundary.
Utilize the getDerivedStateFromError lifecycle method to update component state when errors occur.
Control error state by setting boolean flags to conditionally render fallback UI.
Define componentDidCatch method to handle error logging and side effects.
Construct fallback UI elements to display when errors are caught by the boundary.
Use the Error Boundary component to wrap other components and catch their errors.
Invoke the Error Boundary in JSX by placing it as a parent wrapper around child components.
Execute conditional rendering to show either normal content or error UI based on component state.
Apply TypeScript generics to properly type Error Boundary state and props.
Store error information in component state for access within the fallback UI.
Return appropriate JSX structures from both normal render and error states.

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added, making them available for use in the component.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState, which are essential for building React components with state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react' using the import statement.

steps.title: Create the main ErrorBoundary component
steps.instruction: Create a class component named ErrorBoundary that extends React.Component. Use TypeScript syntax with proper typing.
steps.hint: Define a class that extends React.Component. You'll need to specify props and state types (you can use interfaces or types). For now, you can use 'any' or create placeholder types.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the ErrorBoundary class component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A class component named ErrorBoundary is defined, extending React.Component with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the ErrorBoundary class component with proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined a class named ErrorBoundary that extends React.Component with TypeScript typing and includes a render method.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ErrorBoundary component isn't properly defined. Remember to create a class component that extends React.Component with TypeScript typing.

steps.title: Define the component's state interface
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary component file, create a TypeScript interface named ErrorBoundaryState that defines the shape of the component's state. The interface should have two properties: 'hasError' (boolean) and 'error' (Error | null).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions. Remember to specify types for both properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a TypeScript interface that properly defines the state structure for the ErrorBoundary component.
successCriteria: The interface must be named 'ErrorBoundaryState' and include both 'hasError: boolean' and 'error: Error | null' properties with correct TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the ErrorBoundaryState interface with the correct property types. This will ensure type safety when working with the component's state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface includes both required properties with the correct TypeScript types: 'hasError: boolean' and 'error: Error | null'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition doesn't match the requirements. Make sure to create an interface named 'ErrorBoundaryState' with both 'hasError' (boolean) and 'error' (Error | null) properties.

steps.title: Initialize the component state
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary component's constructor, initialize the state with hasError set to false and error set to null.
steps.hint: In the constructor, call super(props) and then set this.state to an object matching the ErrorBoundaryState interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has its initial state properly set in the constructor.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've correctly initialized the component state with hasError: false and error: null.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're setting this.state to an object with both hasError and error properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization is missing or incorrect. Check that you're setting this.state in the constructor with the correct properties.

steps.title: Implement the getDerivedStateFromError lifecycle method
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary class component, add a static method named getDerivedStateFromError that takes an error parameter and returns an object with hasError set to true and error set to the provided error.
steps.hint: This static method should be placed inside the class body, before the constructor. It receives an error and returns the new state object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a static getDerivedStateFromError method that will update the component's state when an error occurs in its child components.
successCriteria: The method should be static, accept an error parameter of type Error, and return an object matching ErrorBoundaryState with hasError: true and error set to the parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've correctly implemented getDerivedStateFromError. This static lifecycle method will be called when an error occurs in any child component, allowing the ErrorBoundary to update its state and prepare to show a fallback UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Is the method static? Does it accept an error parameter of type Error? Does it return an object with hasError: true and error set to the parameter?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add a static method called getDerivedStateFromError inside the ErrorBoundary class. It should take an error parameter and return { hasError: true, error: error }.

steps.title: Implement the componentDidCatch lifecycle method
steps.instruction: Add the componentDidCatch lifecycle method to your ErrorBoundary class. This method should log the error and errorInfo to the console.
steps.hint: componentDidCatch is an instance method that receives two parameters: error and errorInfo. Use console.log or console.error to log them.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a componentDidCatch method that logs error details to the console.
successCriteria: The componentDidCatch method is defined with the correct parameters (error and errorInfo) and logs them to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the componentDidCatch lifecycle method. This method will be called when an error occurs in any child component, allowing you to log error details for debugging.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your componentDidCatch method has the correct parameters (error: Error, errorInfo: React.ErrorInfo) and logs both values to the console.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on adding just the componentDidCatch method. It should be an instance method in your ErrorBoundary class that logs the error and errorInfo parameters to the console.

steps.title: Create the render method for ErrorBoundary
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary class, add a render method that conditionally returns UI based on the error state. When hasError is true, return an error message UI; otherwise, return the children.
steps.hint: Use this.state.hasError to check the error state. Return JSX with an error message when true, and this.props.children when false.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a render method that conditionally renders error UI or children based on the error state.
successCriteria: The render method should check this.state.hasError and return appropriate JSX. When hasError is true, return error UI (e.g., a div with an error message). When false, return this.props.children.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the render method with conditional rendering based on the error state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a render method, but it might not be checking this.state.hasError correctly or returning the appropriate JSX for both cases. Make sure to return error UI when hasError is true and this.props.children when false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The render method is missing or doesn't follow the required structure. Add a render method that conditionally returns UI based on this.state.hasError.

steps.title: Create a BuggyComponent to test the error boundary
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named BuggyComponent that intentionally throws an error when rendered.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function called BuggyComponent that returns JSX, but include code that will throw an error (e.g., throw new Error('Test error')).
steps.expectedOutcome: A BuggyComponent function that throws an error when rendered, which will be used to test the error boundary.
successCriteria: The code must define a functional component named BuggyComponent that throws an error (e.g., using throw new Error()).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a BuggyComponent that will intentionally throw an error, allowing us to test the error boundary.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but it might not throw an error as required. Make sure BuggyComponent includes code that throws an error (e.g., throw new Error('Test error')).
steps.feedbackWrong: The BuggyComponent is missing or doesn't throw an error. Create a functional component named BuggyComponent that throws an error when rendered.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns an empty JSX element (like a div). This will be the main container for our error boundary test.
steps.hint: Define a function called App that returns a JSX element. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional App component is created that will serve as the main container for the error boundary test.
successCriteria: The code should define a component named App that returns a JSX element (like a div).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the App component. This will be the main container where we'll place our error boundary and buggy component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined a component named App that returns a JSX element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component wasn't created correctly. Make sure to define a function or arrow function named App that returns a JSX element like a div.

steps.title: Initialize state in App component for controlling error
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'showBuggy' with its setter function. Initialize it to true so the BuggyComponent is initially visible.
steps.hint: Remember to import useState if not already imported (it is). Use TypeScript generics to specify the state type as boolean.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now has a state variable 'showBuggy' initialized to true, which will be used to control whether the BuggyComponent is rendered.
successCriteria: The App component should include a useState call that declares a state variable named 'showBuggy' with type boolean and initial value true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the state variable that will control whether the BuggyComponent is shown. This is a crucial step for testing the error boundary.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've properly initialized the state. Check that you've used useState<boolean>(true) and named the variable 'showBuggy' with its setter function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component doesn't have the required state initialization. You need to add a useState hook inside the App component to create a 'showBuggy' state variable initialized to true.

steps.title: Create handler function to trigger the error
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, create a handler function named handleTriggerError that sets the state variable to true.
steps.hint: Define a function that calls the state setter function with the value true.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a handler function that can be used to trigger the error by setting the showBuggy state to true.
successCriteria: The code should define a function named handleTriggerError inside the App component that calls setShowBuggy(true).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the handler function that will trigger the error when called.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named handleTriggerError and it calls setShowBuggy(true).
steps.feedbackWrong: The handler function is missing or incorrect. Create a function named handleTriggerError that calls setShowBuggy(true).

steps.title: Implement the App component JSX with error boundary
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, add JSX that includes the ErrorBoundary wrapping the BuggyComponent conditionally when showBuggy is true, and add a button with an onClick handler that calls the setShowBuggy function to show the buggy component.
steps.hint: Use the ErrorBoundary component as a wrapper around BuggyComponent. Conditionally render BuggyComponent inside ErrorBoundary based on the showBuggy state. Add a button that triggers setShowBuggy(true) when clicked.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component should now render a button that, when clicked, displays the BuggyComponent wrapped inside the ErrorBoundary, allowing you to test the error boundary functionality.
successCriteria: The JSX includes: 1) ErrorBoundary component wrapping BuggyComponent, 2) Conditional rendering of BuggyComponent based on showBuggy state, 3) A button with onClick handler that calls setShowBuggy(true).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully wired up the error boundary test interface. The ErrorBoundary now wraps the BuggyComponent conditionally, and the button triggers the display of the buggy component to test error catching.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but some elements are missing. Make sure you have: 1) ErrorBoundary wrapping BuggyComponent, 2) Conditional rendering using showBuggy state, 3) A button with onClick that calls setShowBuggy(true).
steps.feedbackWrong: The JSX structure doesn't match the requirements. Check that you're using ErrorBoundary as a wrapper, conditionally rendering BuggyComponent inside it based on showBuggy state, and adding a button with the correct onClick handler.
